# Clanker Slack gateway PRD **Status: Draft for user review. No implementation or provisioning authorized by this document.** **Date:** 2026-10-04 **Product contract:** One shared Slack gateway routes authorized tasks to isolated Hermes runtimes. The user experience determines the integration; adapt Hermes where necessary. ## 1. Review decisions 1. **Initial transport and host:** retain Socket Mode in one persistent Python gateway container on Cloudflare, provisionally. HTTP Events API on Workers remains an alternative, not a requirement for dynamic worker dispatch. 2. **Worker integration:** prefer Hermes's existing asynchronous runs API behind a trusted worker wrapper. Adapt the shared gateway's dispatch lifecycle rather than assuming the stock Slack adapter can dispatch dynamically unchanged. Experimental relay remains an alternative if the runs API cannot support the required controls. 3. **Initial Slack surfaces:** 1:1 DMs and explicitly admitted channels/threads; channel tasks require a bot mention. Reject MPIMs, Slack Connect/external senders and unknown audiences in v1. Preserve threaded replies, progress, clarification, approval and cancellation; broad native command parity is not required. 4. **Capacity policy:** bounded configurable workers, fair queuing between contexts, one active run per profile, and sequential ordinary turns within a profile. Queue later turns; owner-authorized cancel/control messages can act on the current task. 5. **Provisioning:** Cloudflare is preferred, but paid capability, budget, instance suitability and persistence behavior must be confirmed before deployment. This draft does not approve spending. These are proposals for review. Existing `MOD_HERMES.md` proposes relay; this draft offers runs API as the initial candidate and does not silently amend that document. ## 2. Problem and intended experience The stock Slack listener and reply code can be useful, but Clanker requires a task to outlive the gateway's current agent invocation and any assigned worker. Receiving ten task events from ten different authorized users must create ten owner/context-scoped tasks. Capacity may run only some immediately; the remainder wait fairly. None share a private Hermes agent, profile mount, browser state or task authority. The gateway is one trusted service. Multiple replicas, maximum throughput discovery and load benchmarking are not v1 prerequisites. One service may include transport and trusted control components; it must not execute arbitrary agent code. ### Concrete journeys | Journey | Required user-visible behavior | | --- | --- | | Private browser task | User DMs a request, sees accepted/queued status, receives useful progress and a verified result in that DM. The assigned worker loads only their authorized context. | | Ten independent users | Ten DM requests become ten distinct tasks tied to the right owners. With a smaller pool, queued users retain their place and eventually receive their own results. | | Shared collaboration | Two admitted participants contribute to one channel thread. They share its authorized conversation context, without loading either participant's private account state. | | Private access during shared work | Shared work identifies a need for Alice's private account. The gateway obtains Alice's authorization privately and creates/links a private task. Private observations return to Alice; sharing selected content requires her exact approval. | | Human input and recovery | A task waits for clarification or a private access form. The worker can be released after a durable checkpoint. Valid input resumes the same task once, even if the prior worker was replaced. | ## 3. Responsibilities and boundaries | Component | Owns | Does not own | | --- | --- | --- | | Shared gateway | Slack connection, admission, authenticated identity, audience mapping, durable task acceptance, safe progress/replies, owner-bound controls | Browser execution, deciding capacity, decrypting vault secrets in chat, arbitrary agent code | | Scheduler/pool manager | Fair dispatch, profile lease, worker assignment, capacity bounds, clean-worker lifecycle, recovery coordination | Deriving human identity from model text, Slack publication authority | | Isolated worker | Hermes, Browser Use driver, local Chromium, scoped profile/files, run events and checkpoints | Broad Slack/cloud credentials, other profiles, independent destination selection | | Durable context store | Versioned authorized history/browser/files and checkpoints beyond worker lifetime | Treating object keys supplied by agents as access grants | | Trusted vault/access service | Slack OIDC, owner/task/site authorization, secure submission, protected storage, durable access-ready signal | Sending passwords/setup keys through Slack, model inputs or queues | The gateway submits an authorized task to the scheduler. The scheduler selects a worker and supplies a scoped assignment. The gateway never assumes an event maps to a permanently allocated user VM. Storage and vault implementation are separate component decisions; this PRD defines their contracts. ```mermaid flowchart LR Slack[Slack] <--> G[One trusted gateway] G --> T[Durable task and delivery records] T --> Q[Queue and scheduler] Q --> W[Assigned isolated worker
Hermes + Browser Use + Chromium] W <--> S[Authorized durable context] W --> R[Bound run events and results] R --> G G <--> V[Trusted access and approval flows] V --> T ``` ## 4. Identity and routing requirements **G1. Authenticated identity.** Derive installation/workspace and sender from the authenticated Slack transport. Socket Mode uses its authenticated connection; HTTP, if selected, verifies the signature against raw bytes and rejects stale requests. Reject unknown installations/workspaces and senders. Model prose, submitted profile names, display names and email addresses confer no authority. **G2. Context selection.** Map a 1:1 DM to an owner-private profile. Map a channel/thread to a profile belonging to its admitted audience, with a thread-specific conversation session. Distinct audiences must not share private memory or browser state. Include tenant identity in every mapping. Fail closed on missing routes; never use a privileged default profile. **G3. Audience admission.** Confirm the channel is admitted and distinguish 1:1 IM from multi-person DM before context selection. Reject unsupported surfaces with a fixed safe response where appropriate. Workspace membership alone does not grant private-channel or personal-context access. Revalidate the permitted destination before delivery; membership/authorization changes suspend affected work for reconciliation. **G4. Distinct authorities.** Track requester, resource owner and output audience separately. Another participant can contribute to shared work without controlling a linked private task, approving an account action, reading private results or cancelling another owner's private run. **G5. Worker confinement.** Mount/load exactly the assigned context and its permitted files/browser state. Agent execution receives neither gateway/platform administrator credentials nor arbitrary storage access. Profile configuration is useful routing machinery, not the security boundary; the prior cross-profile session-search finding remains a release constraint. ## 5. Trusted envelopes These are required semantics, not a frozen wire schema. Trusted components construct and validate identity and routing fields; worker output cannot change them. | Envelope | Required semantics | | --- | --- | | Accepted event | Schema version, authenticated installation/tenant/workspace, sender, surface classification, channel/thread/message IDs, transport event identity, semantic duplicate identity, received time and normalized intent/input or scoped attachment references | | Task | Stable task ID, event association, requester, owner when applicable, authorized context/profile and conversation session, fixed permitted destination/audience, task kind, state/version, parent/private-task association when relevant, checkpoint reference and approved access handles | | Assignment | Task ID, run/attempt ID, context ID, lease and fencing generation, worker identity, scoped state references/version, bounded execution policy and authenticated callback/control capability | | Worker event/result | Task/run/attempt IDs, assigned worker and fencing generation, monotonic event sequence, event kind, safe progress/result or scoped artifact/checkpoint references, verified outcome evidence and failure/uncertainty classification | | Approval/input | Opaque request ID, task/run association, intended owner, exact action or input purpose, immutable content/action digest, audience where sharing is requested, expiry and single-use decision state | Accept callbacks only from the assigned authenticated worker and current generation. Reject stale/wrong-task output. Treat worker event text as untrusted content and apply disclosure rules before Slack delivery. Do not place credentials, broad bearer tokens or secrets in task messages or logs. ## 6. Acceptance, deduplication and ordering **G6. Durable acceptance before success.** Persist the accepted event and task/dispatch intent before acknowledging a task event. If persistence fails, do not claim acceptance. Keep transport acknowledgement within Slack's three-second budget; worker startup and model calls occur later. Unsupported/no-op events may be acknowledged without creating tasks. **G7. Two levels of deduplication.** Repeated transport delivery resolves to the original acceptance record. Also merge Slack `message` and `app_mention` notifications for the same underlying message. Do not collapse an intentional edit or separate user message. Use transport-specific interaction/command identities and make control consumption idempotent. Deduplication must survive gateway restart; the stock in-memory TTL cache is insufficient. **G8. Recoverable dispatch.** Persist acceptance and an outbox/dispatch intent together or use an equivalent recoverable transition. Queue publication failure leaves a retryable accepted task. Queue redelivery does not launch another active attempt. A duplicate event receives success once its original durable acceptance is known. **G9. Profile serialization.** Scheduler leases permit one active run per profile, including shared profiles with multiple thread sessions. Preserve accepted turn order within that profile. Fairly service independent contexts under configured capacity; a busy user cannot monopolize all slots. Throughput ceilings and multi-gateway routing are deferred. ## 7. Progress, replies and controls **G10. Delivery association.** Every progress, clarification, artifact and completion belongs to a task/run and server-selected destination. Socket Mode is inbound transport; replies still use Slack APIs. Workers return events/results to the gateway rather than directly posting to Slack. **G11. Durable delivery.** Record delivery intent and outcome separately from execution. Retry rate-limited/transient Slack failures with bounded backoff and respect Slack retry guidance. Restarting the gateway must not launch the browser task merely because its reply was undelivered. Reconcile ambiguous sends where possible; retain unresolved delivery status rather than claiming exactly-once Slack publication. **G12. Useful status.** Show accepted/queued state, meaningful progress, waiting reason, completion, cancellation or actionable failure. Coalesce repetitive progress. Do not claim an account action succeeded from a generated answer alone; completion requires worker outcome evidence or an explicit uncertain result. **G13. Owner-bound approval.** Validate authenticated clicker against the durable approval owner and current task/run. Bind consequential execution approval to the exact action; changed details require a new request. Private-result sharing approval additionally binds exact content/artifacts and destination audience. Tool permission approval alone is not publication consent. Enforce expiry and single consumption; denied, foreign and replayed decisions cannot resume execution. **G14. Cancellation.** An authorized owner may cancel their private task; shared task controls follow an explicit requester/owner policy, proposed as task requester only for v1. Queued cancellation prevents dispatch. Running cancellation reaches the assigned run and revokes further execution authority. Report `cancelling` until stop is observed, and disclose any external action already performed or whose outcome is uncertain. Late callbacks cannot revive a cancelled task. ## 8. Human input, persistence and recovery **G15. Waiting input.** Persist request purpose, owner, task and expiry outside the worker. Clarification text can use its admitted Slack surface; account secrets use the separate secure access flow. An access-ready signal carries a safe handle, never a password. Atomically consume valid input and record readiness once. Reject mismatched/expired/replayed input; input arriving after cancellation does not resume work. **G16. Worker release.** A waiting worker may be released only after a durable task/checkpoint transition. Run and approval state held only in process memory cannot justify scale-down. Resuming on another worker re-establishes the pending intent from persisted state; do not assume an old in-memory approval resolver survives replacement. **G17. Context persistence.** At task start, load the authorized durable context version. Checkpoint history, browser state and files consistently at defined safe points and before clean release. Use lease/fencing validation for checkpoint publication. Close/flush SQLite and browser state, or use a supported consistent snapshot; copying live files is not established as safe. Never reuse a dirty private worker for another context without verified reset/replacement. **G18. Failure classification.** Track accepted, queued, preparing, running, waiting-for-input/approval, cancelling, completed, failed, cancelled and needs-reconciliation states, with durable transition versions. A worker outage makes the current attempt interrupted. Requeue only after reconciling its lease, checkpoint and possible external effects. Uncertain purchase/post/delete outcomes require verification or owner input, not blind replay. A stored browser session is not a restored live page or unfinished action. ## 9. Hermes reuse and modification boundary Source findings refer to Hermes 0.21.5, tag `v2026.9.24`, commit `f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f`. Paths are under `.local/hermes-lab/upstream/`; these findings do not establish a deployed pass. | Source-verified capability/gap | Intended treatment | | --- | --- | | Slack `connect()` starts Bolt Socket Mode; registered listeners cover messages, mentions, commands and actions (`plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py:1601,1771`). | Reuse listener/reply functionality where it fits. Keep it in a normal Python runtime. Adapt dispatch and trusted controls; transport need not change. | | Message builder derives sender/team/session source, with known MPIM and route pitfalls (Slack audit). | Reuse normalization selectively, enforce G1–G5 before hydration/dispatch. Do not trust stock private/shared classification unchanged. | | Simple proxy mode posts text/history to `/v1/chat/completions` and consumes text SSE (`gateway/run_turn.py:2744`). | It proves remote invocation exists, but does not implement dynamic pool assignment, task persistence or owner-bound controls. Do not declare the architecture solved by configuring it. | | Runs API supports asynchronous admission, status/events, approval, steer/stop and durable idempotency (`gateway/platforms/api_server_runs.py:186`). | Candidate worker boundary. Use per-context authenticated scopes, stable idempotency/session IDs and a trusted wrapper enforcing task/lease association. Verify available capabilities against the pinned worker. | | Run ownership is checked by authenticated API scope; exact approval request IDs are supported (`api_server_runs.py:977,1072`). | Map Slack identity/owner to task authority in the trusted gateway. API scope is not automatically a Slack owner. | | Stock Slack duplicate cache is process memory; approval buttons gate on bot admission (Slack audit; `gateway/platforms/helpers.py:20`). | Add durable deduplication and owner-bound approvals. Reuse display components only after control semantics are adapted. | | Experimental RelayAdapter exchanges normalized events/actions with an external connector. Referenced connector repository was not publicly resolvable. | Alternative extension seam if runs integration fails a required journey. No requirement to rewrite the complete connector or adopt relay before testing the smaller candidate. | The shared gateway needs an adapted task lifecycle: normalize/admit → persist task → scheduler dispatch → bound worker events → durable delivery. Stock adapter use unchanged is not sufficient for that lifecycle. The precise patch/plugin boundary follows focused source validation during implementation, after PRD approval. ## 10. Provisional Cloudflare mapping | Responsibility | Initial candidate | Caveat | | --- | --- | --- | | One persistent Slack transport | Cloudflare Container running adapted Python Slack gateway, Socket Mode | Paid capability and reliable persistent-connection lifecycle unverified; Slack transport reconnects must preserve durable task state. | | Trusted task/control APIs and access UI | Workers | Keep arbitrary Hermes/browser execution outside Workers. Access/vault internals are separate scope. | | Dispatch and coordination | Queues plus Durable Object scheduler/profile leases and durable structured records | Queue delivery is at least once; scheduling, ordering and fencing are application responsibilities. Choose an authoritative record store explicitly. | | Isolated task runtime | Assigned Cloudflare Container, subject to proving required execution isolation | Validate that the offered isolation meets the selected worker boundary; do not call every container a verified VM sandbox. | | Durable scoped profile/browser/files | R2 with versioned manifests/checkpoints, provisionally | Object storage is not a live POSIX/SQLite/browser-profile mount. Restore/checkpoint integration and crash consistency require proof. | **Rationale:** retaining Socket Mode preserves existing adapter behavior and avoids making an HTTP rewrite the first prerequisite. Dynamic authorized dispatch is the actual change. A persistent gateway is acceptable for v1. If container availability/cost or the reuse experiment defeats this approach, switch to HTTP ingress on Workers and retain the same task contracts. Slack HTTP ingress requires signature validation and three-second acknowledgement independently of backend startup. Costs include paid container running resources, Workers/Durable Objects, storage/queue usage and worker capacity. No cost total is asserted without account capability and workload checks. Do not provision a paid plan from approval of this document alone. ## 11. Minimal v1 acceptance All scenarios below are **pending**. Record pinned versions, real versus synthetic environment, observed task/context/run IDs, assertions, failure evidence and limitations. Reuse the evidence ledger in `VERIFICATION_STRATEGY.md`. | Check | Required evidence | Environment | | --- | --- | --- | | A1: Ten distinct owners | Ten authenticated input events produce ten distinct owner/context-scoped tasks; bounded pool dispatches fairly; each result maps correctly; no concurrent runs for one profile. This is a correctness scenario, not a throughput benchmark. | Synthetic transport/worker test initially; label it synthetic. Real two-user checks below remain required. | | A2: Real private/shared routing | Two real Slack users complete concurrent DMs and contribute in a shared thread. Verify histories/destinations and rejection of foreign tenant, unknown route and unsupported MPIM without private worker dispatch. | Real Slack for normal paths; synthetic identities for unavailable tenant/surface negatives. | | A3: Duplicate and restart acceptance | Replay a task envelope and message/mention pair; crash between acceptance/queue publish; restart gateway. One accepted task remains recoverably dispatchable without duplicate active execution. | Controlled failure injection with synthetic transport; real Slack delivery smoke. | | A4: Owner controls and sharing | B cannot approve/cancel A's private work. Owner's expired/replayed/changed-action decision is rejected. A privately reviews exact result content and explicitly approves its shared destination before publication. | Synthetic negative tests plus real two-user Slack interaction journey. | | A5: Access resume and worker replacement | Wait for secure input, checkpoint/release worker, save authorized dummy access, resume the original task once on a replacement worker with scoped history/browser/files. Late input cannot revive cancellation. | Real Slack/access UI and isolated browser workers, dummy account data. | | A6: Delivery and uncertain actions | Worker completion followed by Slack failure/restart retries delivery without rerunning the task. A lost external-action response enters reconciliation and does not automatically replay the action. Cancellation rejects late output. | Controlled failure injection; real Slack/browser confirmation where applicable. | | A7: Runtime boundary | Agent code cannot read another owner's profile/browser/files, broad Slack/cloud credentials or trusted vault keys. Retest the cross-profile recall reproduction within the chosen execution boundary. | Actual deployed worker runtime with dummy secrets and adversarial probes. | Passing mocked source tests or one owner's tool-free Slack inference does not satisfy these journeys. No maximum-load experiment, multiple gateway replicas or full public SaaS onboarding is required to accept v1. ## 12. Scope limits and implementation entry This PRD covers the gateway experience and integration boundaries. It does not select the model funding arrangement, implement the vault, settle manual versus automatic TOTP, define the full VM/provider isolation design, add billing/onboarding, or require deferred operator/provider privacy controls. Those decisions remain in their own component scope. After user review, first prove one accepted DM can be durably dispatched through the candidate worker API and returned to its original destination, including a denied foreign approval and one restart. Audience admission.** Confirm the channel is admitted and distinguish 1:1 IM from multi-person DM before context selection. Reject unsupported surfaces with a fixed safe response where appropriate. Workspace membership alone does not grant private-channel or personal-context access. Revalidate the permitted destination before delivery; membership/authorization changes suspend affected work for reconciliation. **G4. Distinct authorities.** Track requester, resource owner and output audience separately. Another participant can contribute to shared work without controlling a linked private task, approving an account action, reading private results or cancelling another owner's private run. **G5. Worker confinement.** Mount/load exactly the assigned context and its permitted files/browser state. Durable acceptance before success.** Persist the accepted event and task/dispatch intent before acknowledging a task event. If persistence fails, do not claim acceptance. Keep transport acknowledgement within Slack's three-second budget; worker startup and model calls occur later. Unsupported/no-op events may be acknowledged without creating tasks. **G7. Two levels of deduplication.** Repeated transport delivery resolves to the original acceptance record. Also merge Slack `message` and `app_mention` notifications for the same underlying message. Do not collapse an intentional edit or separate user message. Use transport-specific interaction/command identities and make control consumption idempotent. Deduplication must survive gateway restart; the stock in-memory TTL cache is insufficient. **G8. Recoverable dispatch.** Persist acceptance and an outbox/dispatch intent together or use an equivalent recoverable transition. Queue publication failure leaves a retryable accepted task. Queue redelivery does not launch another active attempt. A duplicate event receives success once its original durable acceptance is known. **G9. Fairly service independent contexts under configured capacity; a busy user cannot monopolize all slots. Throughput ceilings and multi-gateway routing are deferred. ## 7. Use per-context authenticated scopes, stable idempotency/session IDs and a trusted wrapper enforcing task/lease association. Progress, replies and controls **G10. Delivery association.** Every progress, clarification, artifact and completion belongs to a task/run and server-selected destination. Socket Mode is inbound transport; replies still use Slack APIs. Workers return events/results to the gateway rather than directly posting to Slack. **G11. Durable delivery.** Record delivery intent and outcome separately from execution. Retry rate-limited/transient Slack failures with bounded backoff and respect Slack retry guidance. Restarting the gateway must not launch the browser task merely because its reply was undelivered. Reconcile ambiguous sends where possible; retain unresolved delivery status rather than claiming exactly-once Slack publication. **G12. Useful status.** Show accepted/queued state, meaningful progress, waiting reason, completion, cancellation or actionable failure. Coalesce repetitive progress. Do not claim an account action succeeded from a generated answer alone; completion requires worker outcome evidence or an explicit uncertain result. **G13. Owner-bound approval.** Validate authenticated clicker against the durable approval owner and current task/run. Bind consequential execution approval to the exact action; changed details require a new request. Private-result sharing approval additionally binds exact content/artifacts and destination audience. Tool permission approval alone is not publication consent. Enforce expiry and single consumption; denied, foreign and replayed decisions cannot resume execution. **G14. Cancellation.** An authorized owner may cancel their private task; shared task controls follow an explicit requester/owner policy, proposed as task requester only for v1. Queued cancellation prevents dispatch. Running cancellation reaches the assigned run and revokes further execution authority. Report `cancelling` until stop is observed, and disclose any external action already performed or whose outcome is uncertain. Late callbacks cannot revive a cancelled task. ## 8. Human input, persistence and recovery **G15. Waiting input.** Persist request purpose, owner, task and expiry outside the worker. Clarification text can use its admitted Slack surface; account secrets use the separate secure access flow. An access-ready signal carries a safe handle, never a password. Atomically consume valid input and record readiness once. Reject mismatched/expired/replayed input; input arriving after cancellation does not resume work. **G16. Worker release.** A waiting worker may be released only after a durable task/checkpoint transition. Run and approval state held only in process memory cannot justify scale-down. Resuming on another worker re-establishes the pending intent from persisted state; do not assume an old in-memory approval resolver survives replacement. **G17. Context persistence.** At task start, load the authorized durable context version. Checkpoint history, browser state and files consistently at defined safe points and before clean release. Use lease/fencing validation for checkpoint publication. Close/flush SQLite and browser state, or use a supported consistent snapshot; copying live files is not established as safe. Never reuse a dirty private worker for another context without verified reset/replacement. **G18. Failure classification.** Track accepted, queued, preparing, running, waiting-for-input/approval, cancelling, completed, failed, cancelled and needs-reconciliation states, with durable transition versions. A worker outage makes the current attempt interrupted. Requeue only after reconciling its lease, checkpoint and possible external effects. Uncertain purchase/post/delete outcomes require verification or owner input, not blind replay. A stored browser session is not a restored live page or unfinished action. ## 9. Hermes reuse and modification boundary Source findings refer to Hermes 0.21.5, tag `v2026.9.24`, commit `f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f`. Paths are under `.local/hermes-lab/upstream/`; these findings do not establish a deployed pass. | Source-verified capability/gap | Intended treatment | | --- | --- | | Slack `connect()` starts Bolt Socket Mode; registered listeners cover messages, mentions, commands and actions (`plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py:1601,1771`). | Reuse listener/reply functionality where it fits. Keep it in a normal Python runtime. Adapt dispatch and trusted controls; transport need not change. | | Message builder derives sender/team/session source, with known MPIM and route pitfalls (Slack audit). | Reuse normalization selectively, enforce G1–G5 before hydration/dispatch. Do not trust stock private/shared classification unchanged. | | Simple proxy mode posts text/history to `/v1/chat/completions` and consumes text SSE (`gateway/run_turn.py:2744`). | It proves remote invocation exists, but does not implement dynamic pool assignment, task persistence or owner-bound controls. Do not declare the architecture solved by configuring it. | | Runs API supports asynchronous admission, status/events, approval, steer/stop and durable idempotency (`gateway/platforms/api_server_runs.py:186`). | Candidate worker boundary. Use per-context authenticated scopes, stable idempotency/session IDs and a trusted wrapper enforcing task/lease association. Verify available capabilities against the pinned worker. | | Run ownership is checked by authenticated API scope; exact approval request IDs are supported (`api_server_runs.py:977,1072`). | Map Slack identity/owner to task authority in the trusted gateway. API scope is not automatically a Slack owner. | | Stock Slack duplicate cache is process memory; approval buttons gate on bot admission (Slack audit; `gateway/platforms/helpers.py:20`). | Add durable deduplication and owner-bound approvals. Reuse display components only after control semantics are adapted. | | Experimental RelayAdapter exchanges normalized events/actions with an external connector. Referenced connector repository was not publicly resolvable. | Alternative extension seam if runs integration fails a required journey. No requirement to rewrite the complete connector or adopt relay before testing the smaller candidate. | The shared gateway needs an adapted task lifecycle: normalize/admit → persist task → scheduler dispatch → bound worker events → durable delivery. Stock adapter use unchanged is not sufficient for that lifecycle. The precise patch/plugin boundary follows focused source validation during implementation, after PRD approval. ## 10. Provisional Cloudflare mapping | Responsibility | Initial candidate | Caveat | | --- | --- | --- | | One persistent Slack transport | Cloudflare Container running adapted Python Slack gateway, Socket Mode | Paid capability and reliable persistent-connection lifecycle unverified; Slack transport reconnects must preserve durable task state. | | Trusted task/control APIs and access UI | Workers | Keep arbitrary Hermes/browser execution outside Workers. Access/vault internals are separate scope. | | Dispatch and coordination | Queues plus Durable Object scheduler/profile leases and durable structured records | Queue delivery is at least once; scheduling, ordering and fencing are application responsibilities. Choose an authoritative record store explicitly. | | Isolated task runtime | Assigned Cloudflare Container, subject to proving required execution isolation | Validate that the offered isolation meets the selected worker boundary; do not call every container a verified VM sandbox. | | Durable scoped profile/browser/files | R2 with versioned manifests/checkpoints, provisionally | Object storage is not a live POSIX/SQLite/browser-profile mount. Restore/checkpoint integration and crash consistency require proof. | **Rationale:** retaining Socket Mode preserves existing adapter behavior and avoids making an HTTP rewrite the first prerequisite. Dynamic authorized dispatch is the actual change. A persistent gateway is acceptable for v1. If container availability/cost or the reuse experiment defeats this approach, switch to HTTP ingress on Workers and retain the same task contracts. Slack HTTP ingress requires signature validation and three-second acknowledgement independently of backend startup. Costs include paid container running resources, Workers/Durable Objects, storage/queue usage and worker capacity. No cost total is asserted without account capability and workload checks. Do not provision a paid plan from approval of this document alone. ## 11. Minimal v1 acceptance All scenarios below are **pending**. Record pinned versions, real versus synthetic environment, observed task/context/run IDs, assertions, failure evidence and limitations. Reuse the evidence ledger in `VERIFICATION_STRATEGY.md`. | Check | Required evidence | Environment | | --- | --- | --- | | A1: Ten distinct owners | Ten authenticated input events produce ten distinct owner/context-scoped tasks; bounded pool dispatches fairly; each result maps correctly; no concurrent runs for one profile. This is a correctness scenario, not a throughput benchmark. | Synthetic transport/worker test initially; label it synthetic. Real two-user checks below remain required. | | A2: Real private/shared routing | Two real Slack users complete concurrent DMs and contribute in a shared thread. Verify histories/destinations and rejection of foreign tenant, unknown route and unsupported MPIM without private worker dispatch. | Real Slack for normal paths; synthetic identities for unavailable tenant/surface negatives. | | A3: Duplicate and restart acceptance | Replay a task envelope and message/mention pair; crash between acceptance/queue publish; restart gateway. One accepted task remains recoverably dispatchable without duplicate active execution. | Controlled failure injection with synthetic transport; real Slack delivery smoke. | | A4: Owner controls and sharing | B cannot approve/cancel A's private work. Owner's expired/replayed/changed-action decision is rejected. A privately reviews exact result content and explicitly approves its shared destination before publication. | Synthetic negative tests plus real two-user Slack interaction journey. | | A5: Access resume and worker replacement | Wait for secure input, checkpoint/release worker, save authorized dummy access, resume the original task once on a replacement worker with scoped history/browser/files. Late input cannot revive cancellation. | Real Slack/access UI and isolated browser workers, dummy account data. | | A6: Delivery and uncertain actions | Worker completion followed by Slack failure/restart retries delivery without rerunning the task. A lost external-action response enters reconciliation and does not automatically replay the action. Cancellation rejects late output. | Controlled failure injection; real Slack/browser confirmation where applicable. | | A7: Runtime boundary | Agent code cannot read another owner's profile/browser/files, broad Slack/cloud credentials or trusted vault keys. Retest the cross-profile recall reproduction within the chosen execution boundary. | Actual deployed worker runtime with dummy secrets and adversarial probes. | Passing mocked source tests or one owner's tool-free Slack inference does not satisfy these journeys. No maximum-load experiment, multiple gateway replicas or full public SaaS onboarding is required to accept v1. ## 12. Scope limits and implementation entry This PRD covers the gateway experience and integration boundaries. It does not select the model funding arrangement, implement the vault, settle manual versus automatic TOTP, define the full VM/provider isolation design, add billing/onboarding, or require deferred operator/provider privacy controls. Those decisions remain in their own component scope. After user review, first prove one accepted DM can be durably dispatched through the candidate worker API and returned to its original destination, including a denied foreign approval and one restart. Then extend to the remaining acceptance journeys. Patch Hermes or introduce custom connector code only for demonstrated contract gaps. **Current blocker:** implementation awaits user review; there is no blocker to reviewing this draft. Cloudflare paid capability, worker boundary/persistence proof and the final adapter/API seam are prerequisites to deployment, not prerequisites to drafting the contract. ## References - [V1 scope](V1_SCOPE.md), [verification strategy](VERIFICATION_STRATEGY.md), [existing Hermes change proposals](MOD_HERMES.md). - [Pinned baseline](verification/hermes/baseline.json), [Slack source audit and probes](verification/audit-slack-notes.md), [isolation audit](verification/ISOLATION_SOURCE_AUDIT.md). - [Pinned Slack adapter](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f/plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py), [pinned runs API](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f/gateway/platforms/api_server_runs.py), [pinned relay contract](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/blob/f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f/website/docs/developer-guide/relay-connector-contract.md). - [Slack Socket Mode](https://docs.slack.dev/apis/events-api/using-socket-mode/), [HTTP Events API](https://docs.slack.dev/apis/events-api/), [request verification](https://docs.slack.dev/authentication/verifying-requests-from-slack/), [interactions](https://docs.slack.dev/interactivity/handling-user-interaction/). - [Cloudflare Containers lifecycle](https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/concepts/architecture/), [Containers pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/containers/platform/pricing/), [Queues guarantees](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/reference/delivery-guarantees/), [Queues external consumers](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/configuration/pull-consumers/).

verification/poc_single_gateway/hooks/clanker-poc/README.md:20:The awaited `agent:start` hook verifies the current profile/home and authoritative gateway context. It runs the stock `_run_browser_command(session_id, "open", ["about:blank"])`, then the stock `eval` command labels only the blank page's title. It finds that exact page through the configured loopback CDP `/json/list` endpoint. It never inserts replacement website content.
verification/poc_single_gateway/hooks/clanker-poc/README.md:28:The recorder attaches to this actual target, starts capture, and only then creates the configured ready file. After the file appears, the hook records `task_execution_start` and returns to the stock agent runner. `agent:step` and `agent:end` add observations; the end hook also records `task_execution_end`.
verification/poc_single_gateway/hooks/clanker-poc/README.md:30:Prewarm/discovery failures write neither a new binding nor target receipt. Gate failures remove receipts belonging to that setup and record `setup_failed`. Hook exceptions are swallowed by stock Hermes, so the public tools must independently reject missing bindings or missing recording readiness. A completed hook is not a replacement for that tool check.

verification/poc_single_gateway/hooks/clanker-poc/README.md:20:The awaited `agent:start` hook verifies the current profile/home and authoritative gateway context. It finds that exact page through the configured loopback CDP `/json/list` endpoint. It never inserts replacement website content.
verification/poc_single_gateway/hooks/clanker-poc/README.md:28:The recorder attaches to this actual target, starts capture, and only then creates the configured ready file. After the file appears, the hook records `task_execution_start` and returns to the stock agent runner. `agent:step` and `agent:end` add observations; the end hook also records `task_execution_end`.
verification/poc_single_gateway/hooks/clanker-poc/README.md:30:Prewarm/discovery failures write neither a new binding nor target receipt. Gate failures remove receipts belonging to that setup and record `setup_failed`. Hook exceptions are swallowed by stock Hermes, so the public tools must independently reject missing bindings or missing recording readiness. A completed hook is not a replacement for that tool check.

# Operator onboarding for the public-task POC

Use the same installed `@clanker` app and the same multiplexed gateway. Sahan and Nishant each need their verified Slack member ID, an operator-created profile, admission permission and an exact route before they have their own profile context. No invitation, member-ID lookup, provisioning or restart for them was performed by this documentation update.

**Observed live:** the successful two-user run used two profiles created by the operator before either mention. It establishes routing and concurrent execution for those preconfigured accounts. **Source review only:** joining the workspace or sending a first authorized mention does not automatically provision a member profile in pinned Hermes `0.21.5` / `f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f`. No live `team_join` or new-reviewer first-contact test was performed.

| Event or state | Pinned stock behavior and evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Slack `team_join` | No named listener; the [registered event list](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py:1621) ends before a [catch-all acknowledgement/ignore handler](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py:1647). A delivered join event does not create a profile. |
| First authorized `@clanker` mention | [Stock intake](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py:1622) builds the [authoritative message source](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py:4580), then resolves existing routes/profiles. The [served-profile roster](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/hermes_cli/profiles.py:1050) is explicitly a pure directory read. A new conversation session is not a new member profile. |
| Unknown, unapproved sender | Both the POC root and restored original root currently allow only `U0C684PHZ5H,U0C688SF7DZ`; no allow-all flag is set. [Allowlist evaluation](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/authz_mixin.py:662) and [inbound denial](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/run_inbound.py:231) reject a sender without an existing admission grant. The [offline real-API probe](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/verification/poc_single_gateway/routing-preflight.json) separately exercised unknown-sender denial. |
| Sender merely added to the allowlist, without a matching route | [No route returns `None`](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/run.py:4483); [identity resolution](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/session_identity.py:250) chooses the primary/default profile. This does not create an owner profile. An explicit route to an unserved profile is instead rejected. |

The caller audit searched all non-test upstream Python for `create_profile` and `team_join`, then separately traced `ensure_setup_profile` callers. Actual `create_profile(...)` callers were the [CLI command](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/hermes_cli/profile_cmd.py:205), [REST create endpoint](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/hermes_cli/web_routers/profiles.py:720), [TUI create method](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tui_gateway/methods_profiles.py:397), and [desktop setup helper](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/hermes_cli/setup_profile.py:74). That helper is called by [desktop onboarding](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/tui_gateway/methods_onboarding.py:11), not Slack ingress. No caller or `team_join` occurrence was found in `gateway/` or `plugins/platforms/slack/`. Combined with the event-handler and route trace above, this supports the scoped negative claim about automatic Slack member provisioning; it is not a claim that Hermes has no profile-creation APIs.

Operator sequence for each reviewer:

1. Verify the member's actual Slack workspace and user ID through Slack, and record the intended test channel. Do not derive identity from prompt text, a display name, or a claimed email.
2. Under the POC's existing isolated `HERMES_HOME`, inspect `hermes profile create --help`, then create a fresh named profile using `--no-alias --no-skills`. Do not clone a personal profile, change the OS `HOME`, or set a sticky active profile. Configure the approved model and public tools in the new profile; leave Slack bot credentials on the root transport profile.
3. Add one exact root `profile_routes` entry combining `platform: slack`, `bot_profile: default`, workspace `guild_id`, test-channel `chat_id`, actual `user_id`, and the new profile name. Add that actual ID to the root `SLACK_ALLOWED_USERS`. Keep the test channel allowlist and `disable_dms: true`; the root/default Slack toolset remains empty.
4. Have the runtime owner apply/reload the route and admission configuration using the supported gateway lifecycle. Stock multiplexing discovers explicitly created live profile directories at startup and on reconciliation; profile creation signals a rescan, and the periodic rescan is every 30 seconds. This discovery is separate from reloading root routing/allowlist settings.
5. Run the offline routing preflight and then submit one harmless top-level `@clanker` request from the newly admitted real account. Inspect the persisted profile/session identity and its own-thread result before admitting further accounts.

Stock unmatched routes fall back to the default profile. They are not automatically rejected. The installed POC public-tool plugin separately checks the authoritative workspace/channel/sender binding before public-tool access; the default Slack toolset is empty. The offline stock-routing probe does not verify that plugin.

Source references in the pinned checkout:

- [Home selection](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/hermes_constants.py:217): custom `HERMES_HOME` outside the native default is the profile root.
- [Explicit creation](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/hermes_cli/profiles.py:1238) and [CLI options](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/hermes_cli/subcommands/profile.py:40): profile creation and `--no-alias`/`--no-skills` meanings.
- [Profile reconciliation](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/run_profile_reconcile.py:29): 30-second rescan of profiles that already exist.
- [Route matching](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/profile_routing.py:74): all declared identity/location discriminators must match.
# One gateway, two real Slack users — 4 October 2026

**Verified:** one stock Hermes gateway OS process, **PID 24871**, handled two fresh `@clanker` mentions through its normal Slack transport, routed them to two profiles and sessions, and completed both public-browser tasks. Hermes was **0.21.5**, pinned to `f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f`. Both replies identify the same installed Slack app `A0C78PBUKQQ` and bot `U0C5Z1ZQHQX`.

This run (`20261004T150208Z`) supersedes the **architecture claim for the current POC** in the [earlier two-process report](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/verification/evidence/2026-10-04-two-user-parallel.md), which remains preserved as a separate experiment. This run used no custom dispatcher or per-task Hermes process.

Both exact stock routes required `platform: slack`, `bot_profile: default`, workspace `T0C6J1XCDE0`, channel `C0C6J277ZNG`, and the respective sender:

| Sender | Profile | Session | Slack thread root |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `U0C684PHZ5H` | `owner-a-public` | `20261004_203507_1a8c0b31` | `1791126304.421969` |
| `U0C688SF7DZ` | `owner-b-public` | `20261004_203507_2f1c9c46` | `1791126304.458099` |

The [runtime audit](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/one-gateway-poc/evidence/runtime-verification.json) binds both executions to PID 24871 and distinct browser targets. Task execution overlapped for **29.115289125 seconds**, excluding prewarming and the recording gate. Browser calls were simultaneously in flight for **1.500409792 seconds**. Intervals use monotonic clocks, with small logging overhead. All **six required navigations succeeded**.

Independent read-only Slack API observation verified both actual senders, serialized bot mentions, complete prompts, thread roots and final replies: [A request](https://clanker-global.slack.com/archives/C0C6J277ZNG/p1791126304421969), [A answer](https://clanker-global.slack.com/archives/C0C6J277ZNG/p1791126348326009), [B request](https://clanker-global.slack.com/archives/C0C6J277ZNG/p1791126304458099), [B answer](https://clanker-global.slack.com/archives/C0C6J277ZNG/p1791126348304539). [Server records](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/one-gateway-poc/evidence/verified-messages.json) and [answer checks](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/one-gateway-poc/evidence/slack-results.json) establish **12/12 Safe/Idempotent facts and 6/6 exact source URLs**, matching both the previous independent oracle and [fresh official MDN HTTPS/table parsing](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/one-gateway-poc/evidence/mdn-oracle-refresh.json).

Two custom extensions used supported plugin/hook mechanisms: a four-tool public-browser wrapper delegates to stock browser handlers while checking task bindings and MDN navigation arguments; a recording hook prepares the session target, waits for capture readiness, and timestamps execution. [Source hashes](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/one-gateway-poc/evidence/source-hash-manifest.json) confirm the upstream checkout was clean and both installed extension copies matched reviewed source.

| Source pointer | Relevant behavior |
| --- | --- |
| [Slack adapter:1622](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/plugins/platforms/slack/adapter.py:1622) | Stock message/app-mention intake |
| [Profile routes:74](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/profile_routing.py:74) | All route discriminators must match |
| [Routing identity:191](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/session_identity.py:191) | Transport and runtime profile binding |
| [Session keys:673](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/session.py:673) | Profile/workspace/channel/thread namespace |
| [Gateway executor:4309](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/run.py:4309) | Context-preserving worker threads |
| [Browser wrapper:143](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/verification/poc_single_gateway/plugins/clanker-public-browser/__init__.py:143) | Checks, stock delegation, tool receipts |
| [Recording hook:196](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/verification/poc_single_gateway/hooks/clanker-poc/handler.py:196) | Target preparation and recording gate |
| [Watchdog:355](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/upstream/gateway/shutdown_watchdog.py:355) | Failed socket bind limits liveness classification |

Observed deviations: both answers used three labeled bullets instead of the requested table; both threads included stock home-channel and onboarding notices. Startup logged **`AF_UNIX path too long`**, disabling the loop-scheduling witness and stale-heartbeat escalation ([log](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/one-gateway-poc/evidence/gateway.log:12)); execution still completed. The [original gateway was restored](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/.local/hermes-lab/one-gateway-poc/evidence/primary-restored.json) as PID **25802**, Slack connected, with `config.yaml`, `.env` and `auth.json` hashes unchanged.

[Watch the 65.4-second narrated video](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Movies/clanker-one-gateway-2026-10-04/verification.mp4): 1920×1080 H.264/30 fps with fresh ElevenLabs Hinglish narration and UTC-aligned **5 fps source footage at 1x**. [Final QA](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Movies/clanker-one-gateway-2026-10-04/final-qa.json) passed source/final decoding and seven frame checks covering all six MDN pages and both Slack results; bottom source URLs partly leave the viewport but remain complete in the linked API records.

Onboarding: the live POC used **operator-precreated profiles**. Source review—not a live join test—shows neither `team_join` nor a first authorized mention creates a member profile. Unknown, unapproved senders are denied; allowlisting without a matching route falls back to `default`. Sahan and Nishant each need a verified member ID, operator-created profile, admission and exact route for their own context through the same installed `@clanker`/gateway ([source trace and plan](/Users/tanishqpalandurkar/Projects/yyot/verification/poc_single_gateway/ONBOARDING_PLAN.md)). No invitations or onboarding were performed for them.

Limits: public tasks do not prove private-resource authorization, OS isolation or hosted deployment. Dedicated public Chrome processes were reused. Runtime receipts establish browsing/overlap; Slack records establish delivery.

"""Execute the stock Hermes CLI with the fresh, isolated POC home."""
import os
from pathlib import Path
import sys

root = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
lab = root / '.local/hermes-lab'
poc = lab / 'one-gateway-poc'
os.umask(0o077)
for name in ('workspace', 'managed', 'gateway-locks'):
    (poc / name).mkdir(exist_ok=True)
env = {key: os.environ[key] for key in ('HOME', 'PATH', 'LANG', 'TERM', 'TMPDIR', 'USER', 'SHELL') if key in os.environ}
env.update(HERMES_HOME=str(poc / 'home'), HERMES_MANAGED_DIR=str(poc / 'managed'),
           HERMES_GATEWAY_LOCK_DIR=str(poc / 'gateway-locks'), HERMES_DISABLE_LAZY_INSTALLS='1',
           HERMES_STARTUP_WARMUP_TIMEOUT='0', PYTHONUNBUFFERED='1')
env['PATH'] = str(lab / 'venv/bin') + os.pathsep + env.get('PATH', '')
os.chdir(poc / 'workspace')
os.execve(str(lab / 'venv/bin/hermes'), ['hermes', *sys.argv[1:]], env)
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Invoke the pinned stock Hermes checkout with dedicated local state.
# This is not a security sandbox; use dummy data for boundary experiments.
set -euo pipefail
umask 077

project_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
lab_dir="$project_dir/.local/hermes-lab"

if [[ ! -x "$lab_dir/venv/bin/hermes" ]]; then
  echo "Install the pinned baseline first; see verification/LOCAL_BASELINE.md." >&2
  exit 1
fi
if [[ -e "$lab_dir/upstream/.env" ]]; then
  echo "The upstream checkout has a fallback .env; keep credentials only in the lab home." >&2
  exit 1
fi

mkdir -p "$lab_dir/home" "$lab_dir/workspace" "$lab_dir/gateway-locks" "$lab_dir/managed"
if [[ ! -f "$lab_dir/home/config.yaml" ]]; then

1:# Clanker Slack gateway PRD
7:## 1. Review decisions
11:3. **Initial Slack surfaces:** 1:1 DMs and explicitly admitted channels/threads; channel tasks require a bot mention. Reject MPIMs, Slack Connect/external senders and unknown audiences in v1. Preserve threaded replies, progress, clarification, approval and cancellation; broad native command parity is not required.
17:## 2. Problem and intended experience
23:### Concrete journeys
29:| Shared collaboration | Two admitted participants contribute to one channel thread. They share its authorized conversation context, without loading either participant's private account state. |
33:## 3. Responsibilities and boundaries
37:| Shared gateway | Slack connection, admission, authenticated identity, audience mapping, durable task acceptance, safe progress/replies, owner-bound controls | Browser execution, deciding capacity, decrypting vault secrets in chat, arbitrary agent code |
39:| Isolated worker | Hermes, Browser Use driver, local Chromium, scoped profile/files, run events and checkpoints | Broad Slack/cloud credentials, other profiles, independent destination selection |
58:## 4. Identity and routing requirements
62:**G2. Context selection.** Map a 1:1 DM to an owner-private profile. Map a channel/thread to a profile belonging to its admitted audience, with a thread-specific conversation session. Distinct audiences must not share private memory or browser state. Include tenant identity in every mapping. Fail closed on missing routes; never use a privileged default profile.
64:**G3. Audience admission.** Confirm the channel is admitted and distinguish 1:1 IM from multi-person DM before context selection. Reject unsupported surfaces with a fixed safe response where appropriate. Workspace membership alone does not grant private-channel or personal-context access. Revalidate the permitted destination before delivery; membership/authorization changes suspend affected work for reconciliation.
70:## 5. Trusted envelopes
76:| Accepted event | Schema version, authenticated installation/tenant/workspace, sender, surface classification, channel/thread/message IDs, transport event identity, semantic duplicate identity, received time and normalized intent/input or scoped attachment references |
84:## 6. Acceptance, deduplication and ordering
94:## 7. Progress, replies and controls
106:## 8. Human input, persistence and recovery
116:## 9. Hermes reuse and modification boundary
118:Source findings refer to Hermes 0.21.5, tag `v2026.9.24`, commit `f97608f178d1ffeca59860195ab7da295f7c8e5f`. Paths are under `.local/hermes-lab/upstream/`; these findings do not establish a deployed pass.
125:| Runs API supports asynchronous admission, status/events, approval, steer/stop and durable idempotency (`gateway/platforms/api_server_runs.py:186`). | Candidate worker boundary. Use per-context authenticated scopes, stable idempotency/session IDs and a trusted wrapper enforcing task/lease association. Verify available capabilities against the pinned worker. |
127:| Stock Slack duplicate cache is process memory; approval buttons gate on bot admission (Slack audit; `gateway/platforms/helpers.py:20`). | Add durable deduplication and owner-bound approvals. Reuse display components only after control semantics are adapted. |
132:## 10. Provisional Cloudflare mapping
146:## 11. Minimal v1 acceptance
162:## 12. Scope limits and implementation entry
170:## References

# Invoke the pinned stock Hermes checkout with dedicated local state.

umask 077

project_dir="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"

if [[ ! -x "$lab_dir/venv/bin/hermes" ]]; then

fi
if [[ -e "$lab_dir/upstream/.env" ]]; then

  exit 1

mkdir -p "$lab_dir/home" "$lab_dir/workspace" "$lab_dir/gateway-locks" "$lab_dir/managed"

auth:

7:## 1. Review decisions
11:3. **Initial Slack surfaces:** 1:1 DMs and explicitly admitted channels/threads; channel tasks require a bot mention. Reject MPIMs, Slack Connect/external senders and unknown audiences in v1. Preserve threaded replies, progress, clarification, approval and cancellation; broad native command parity is not required.
17:## 2. Problem and intended experience
23:### Concrete journeys
29:| Shared collaboration | Two admitted participants contribute to one channel thread. They share its authorized conversation context, without loading either participant's private account state. |
33:## 3. Responsibilities and boundaries
37:| Shared gateway | Slack connection, admission, authenticated identity, audience mapping, durable task acceptance, safe progress/replies, owner-bound controls | Browser execution, deciding capacity, decrypting vault secrets in chat, arbitrary agent code |
39:| Isolated worker | Hermes, Browser Use driver, local Chromium, scoped profile/files, run events and checkpoints | Broad Slack/cloud credentials, other profiles, independent destination selection |
58:## 4. Identity and routing requirements
62:**G2. Context selection.** Map a 1:1 DM to an owner-private profile. Map a channel/thread to a profile belonging to its admitted audience, with a thread-specific conversation session. Distinct audiences must not share private memory or browser state. Include tenant identity in every mapping. Fail closed on missing routes; never use a privileged default profile.
64:**G3. Audience admission.** Confirm the channel is admitted and distinguish 1:1 IM from multi-person DM before context selection. Reject unsupported surfaces with a fixed safe response where appropriate. Workspace membership alone does not grant private-channel or personal-context access. Revalidate the permitted destination before delivery; membership/authorization changes suspend affected work for reconciliation.

76:| Accepted event | Schema version, authenticated installation/tenant/workspace, sender, surface classification, channel/thread/message IDs, transport event identity, semantic duplicate identity, received time and normalized intent/input or scoped attachment references |

item.stdout:
# One-gateway public browser POC plugin

Install this directory under each POC profile's `plugins/`. It registers only
`public_browser_navigate`, `public_browser_snapshot`, `public_browser_scroll`, and
`public_browser_back`, which delegate to the pinned Hermes stock handlers.

Each profile requires:

```yaml
browser:
  backend: "off"
  cdp_url: "http://127.0.0.1:50388" # B uses 50389
plugins:
  enabled: [clanker-public-browser]
platform_toolsets:
  slack: [public_browser, no_mcp]
tools:
  tool_search:
    enabled: "off"
context:
  engine: compressor
poc:
  expected_user_id: "THE_VERIFIED_SLACK_USER_ID"
  channel_id: "THE_AUTHORIZED_SLACK_CHANNEL_ID"
```

Keep process-global `BROWSER_CDP_URL` unset. Extra plugins, MCP configuration or
tools make the inventory check fail closed before browser execution.

Before the agent's first tool call, the gateway hook must write
`<profile-home>/poc-bindings/<session_id>.json` with these string fields:

```json
{
  "session_id": "gateway session id",
  "profile": "profile name from the scoped Hermes home",
  "user_id": "authenticated Slack sender",
  "chat_id": "authorized channel",
  "thread_id": "original message/thread timestamp",
  "recording_ready_file": "/absolute/path/to/the/recorders/ready-marker"
}
```

The hook owns this file and the recorder owns the ready marker. The plugin never
creates either. Both dispatcher kwargs (`task_id` and `session_id`) must equal the
binding session. User, channel, thread and profile must also match Hermes's
gateway context. No identity or endpoint field exists in the model-facing schemas.

`poc-events.jsonl` in the current profile records `tool_registration`,
`tool_inventory`, `tool_denied`, `tool_start` and `tool_complete`. Every record has
UTC, monotonic nanoseconds, PID, Python thread ID, scoped profile/home and task ID.
Started/completed calls share `call_id`; completions retain the public stock result.
`slack_thread_id` is the Slack timestamp; `thread_id` is the Python thread ID.
The inventory receipt is the configured model-tool schema inventory; it does not
claim inspection of any later agent-added tools.

The navigation guard permits only HTTPS `developer.mozilla.org` URLs without
userinfo or nonstandard ports. Existing browser tabs/history must already contain
only public test state. This POC does not enforce network containment, private
login authorization, OS isolation, or separate browser state for two tasks using
the same profile endpoint.

Offline verification: run `verification/poc_single_gateway/check_plugin.py` with
the pinned Hermes Python environment. It loads this plugin through real discovery
in two temporary homes, verifies the exact schemas and binding/recording gates,
and checks scoped dispatch using explicit stock-handler spies. It forbids network
connections and performs no actual browser or model calls.

L189: By default, local browsing runs in a clean, throwaway profile — the agent is logged into nothing. Turn on real profile browsing to let the agent browse as you, with your existing logins and cookies:
L190: 
L191:     `
L192: 
L193:     # ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L194: 
L195:     browser:
L196: 
L197:       use_real_profile: true
L198: 
L199:     `
L200: When enabled, Hermes copies your default browser's active profile — the one you actually browse (`Local State → profile.last_used`), with its cookies, saved logins, and preferences — into a managed snapshot under `~/.hermes/browser-profile/<browser>/`, then launches your real browser binary on that snapshot and attaches its browsing engine to it.
L201: Launching the real binary (instead of a bundled Chromium with mock-keychain switches) is what keeps OS-encrypted cookies decryptable — on macOS, Chrome cookies are encrypted through the Keychain, and a mock-keychain launch would silently drop every one of them, opening signed out.
L202: Your live browser profile is never opened directly: the snapshot is a separate directory, so it doesn't fight your running browser for the profile lock and it sidesteps Chrome 136+'s block on remote-debugging the default profile directory. The auth files (cookies/logins/preferences) are re-synced from your real profile whenever a fresh session is launched, so logins you do in your own browser show up in the agent's session. Only the active profile is copied — other Chrome profiles are never snapshotted.
L203: The snapshot browser runs headless — it drives your profile in the background with no visible window and never steals focus, so you can keep working while the agent tweets, fills forms, or scrapes on your behalf. (Headless here uses Chrome's new headless mode, which reads your normal cookie store, so your logins still load.) If you'd rather watch it work, the same cite49†headed-mode toggle applies — `browser.headed: true` (or `AGENT_BROWSER_HEADED=1`) opens a visible window for real-profile browsing too.
L204: On a display-less host (servers, CI) it always runs headless regardless.
L205: If your browser has several profiles (say a work profile and a personal one) and you don't want "whichever profile you touched last" deciding the agent's identity, pin the snapshot source explicitly:
L206: 
L207:     `
L208: 
L209:     # ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L210: 
L211:     browser:
L212: 
L213:       use_real_profile: true
L214: 
L215:       real_profile_pin: "Profile 2"   # directory name under the browser's user-data dir
L216: 
L217:     `
L218: A pin naming a profile directory that doesn't exist fails closed with a fixable message — it never silently falls back to the last-used profile.
L219: 
L220: When you turn the toggle back off, Hermes deletes the snapshot store (`~/.hermes/browser-profile/`) on the next browser use, so the copied credentials don't linger after you revoke consent.
L221: 
L222: A running browser can block the login/autofill databases
L223: On Windows a running Chrome/Edge/Brave holds its cookie and login databases with an exclusive (deny-all) lock, so Hermes cannot copy them while the browser is open — it fails fast with a "fully quit the browser and retry" message rather than hang or produce a signed-out session. Real-profile browsing on Windows therefore requires the browser fully quit, including any background/tray instance (Chrome's "continue running background apps when closed" keeps a `chrome.exe` alive after you close the window).
L224: On macOS and Linux the profile is not file-locked, but each authentication database is snapshotted through SQLite's online backup with a five-second budget, and a running Chrome typically holds `Login Data`, `Login Data For Account` and `Web Data` with a hot write lock that never yields within that budget (`Cookies` usually snapshots fine).
L225: When that happens Hermes stops the launch and names the databases it could not read — for example "chrome is running and holds the profile's Login Data, Login Data For Account, Web Data with a write lock" — so in practice quit the browser before launching a real-profile session on macOS/Linux too. You can reopen it once the session is up (the snapshot is a separate directory), but the auth files are re-synced on every fresh session launch, so a browser left running then hits the same lock.
L226: Hermes preserves committed WAL data through SQLite rather than falling back to a raw file copy, which could silently lose recent logins. Unreadable or corrupt databases also stop the launch, with the SQLite error named in the message.
L227: Set `browser.real_profile_autoclose: true` to let Hermes offer to close the browser for you when it's holding the profile lock (the Windows case). Even with this on, Hermes never closes it automatically — when the profile is locked it always stops and the agent asks you first; only on your approval does it run `hermes browser close-profile` (terminates the browser process tree bound to that profile, losing unsaved tabs), then retries. If the profile is still locked after that (e.g.
L228: a background/tray instance relaunched), Hermes stays blocked and tells you to fully quit the browser — it won't loop or kill again on its own.
L229:   * Supported browsers: Chrome, Edge, Brave, Brave Origin, Chromium (whichever is your OS default). A non-Chromium default (e.g. Firefox) fails closed with a clear message rather than guessing.
L230:   * Works on any backend. On a local backend it's automatic once the toggle is on. Under a cloud browser backend, the agent can still open a real-profile local session on demand via the `browser_exec` tool's `local` argument (the tool only exposes that argument when this toggle is on) — the cloud backend keeps serving everything else.
L231:   * Security framing: this is a consent-gated convenience, not an isolation boundary. A page the agent visits runs with your real logins, so only enable it when you want the agent acting as you. Off by default.
L232:   * Desktop: toggle it in Capabilities → Tools → Browser → Use My Real Browser Profile (the switch sits above the backend options), or in Settings → Config under the `browser` section.
L233: #### Scheduled and unattended runscite50†​ L234: 
L235: A real-profile session lets a `cronjob` drive a site you're already signed into. The snapshot runs headless by default, and the auth files (`Cookies`, `Login Data`, …) are re-synced from your real profile on every fresh session — an already-open session is reused as-is, so the sync happens when a new one is launched. Without saved vault credentials, an expired session on that site surfaces as a login page that the unattended tick reports rather than hanging on.
L236: Three things to set up before scheduling one:
L237:   * Turn the toggle on. `browser.use_real_profile` defaults to `false`, and without it the job gets a clean, unauthenticated profile — see above.
L238:   * Give the job the browser toolset: `cronjob(action="create", enabled_toolsets=["browser", ...], ...)` — a per-job list wins over the cron-platform config (cite51†details ).
L239:   * Assume nothing can be prompted for. A cron, webhook, API or `hermes chat -q` session has nobody to answer a prompt, so a site that is not usable on the synced cookies alone — a login form, a fresh 2FA challenge — needs its credentials saved ahead of time, authenticator key included. That is the cite52†credential vault's job, and it is what carries a run after your own session has expired.
L240: Windows prerequisite: the browser has to be fully quit before a snapshot can be taken at all, so a scheduled tick needs it closed beforehand — Hermes never closes it without asking you first (see the note above).
L241: 
L242: The bundled `product-price-monitor` skill is a worked example of the recurring shape — a JSON watch contract written during setup, then one scheduled tick that re-reads it, compares, and alerts on change — though it covers the scheduling half, not logins.

L364: #### Persistent browser sessionscite54†​ L365: 
L366: By default, each Camofox session gets a random identity — cookies and logins don't survive across agent restarts. To enable persistent browser sessions, add the following to `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:
L367: 
L368:     `
L369: 
L370:     browser:
L371: 
L372:       camofox:
L373: 
L374:         managed_persistence: true
L375: 
L376:     `
L377: 
L378: Then fully restart Hermes so the new config is picked up.
L379: 
L380: Nested path matters
L381: Hermes reads `browser.camofox.managed_persistence`, not a top-level `managed_persistence`. A common mistake is writing:
L382: 
L383:     `
L384: 
L385:     # ❌ Wrong — Hermes ignores this
L386: 
L387:     managed_persistence: true
L388: 
L389:     `
L390: 
L391: If the flag is placed at the wrong path, Hermes silently falls back to a random ephemeral `userId` and your login state will be lost on every session.
L392: ##### What Hermes doescite55†​ L393: 
L394:   * Sends a deterministic profile-scoped `userId` to Camofox so the server can reuse the same Firefox profile across sessions.
L395:   * Skips server-side context destruction on cleanup, so cookies and logins survive between agent tasks.
L396:   * Scopes the `userId` to the active Hermes profile, so different Hermes profiles get different browser profiles (profile isolation).
L397: ##### What Hermes does not docite56†​ L398: 
L399:   * It does not force persistence on the Camofox server. Hermes only sends a stable `userId`; the server must honor it by mapping that `userId` to a persistent Firefox profile directory.
L400:   * If your Camofox server build treats every request as ephemeral (e.g. always calls `browser.newContext()` without loading a stored profile), Hermes cannot make those sessions persist. Make sure you are running a Camofox build that implements userId-based profile persistence.
L401: ##### Verify it's workingcite57†​ L402: 
L403:   1. Start Hermes and your Camofox server.
L404:   2. Open Google (or any login site) in a browser task and sign in manually.
L405:   3. End the browser task normally.
L406:   4. Start a new browser task.
L407:   5. Open the same site again — you should still be signed in.
L408: If step 5 logs you out, the Camofox server isn't honoring the stable `userId`. Double-check your config path, confirm you fully restarted Hermes after editing `config.yaml`, and verify your Camofox server version supports persistent per-user profiles.
L409: ##### Where state livescite58†​ L410: 
L411: Hermes derives the stable `userId` from the profile-scoped directory `~/.hermes/browser_auth/camofox/` (or the equivalent under `$HERMES_HOME` for non-default profiles). The actual browser profile data lives on the Camofox server side, keyed by that `userId`. To fully reset a persistent profile, clear it on the Camofox server and remove the corresponding Hermes profile's state directory.
L412: #### Externally managed Camofox sessionscite59†​ L413: 
L414: When another app drives the visible Camofox browser (a desktop assistant, a custom integration, another agent), configure Hermes to operate inside that same identity instead of spawning its own isolated profile.
L415: 
L416: Three knobs control the behavior:
L417: Setting  | Env var  | Effect
L418: --- | --- | ---
L419: `browser.camofox.user_id`  | `CAMOFOX_USER_ID`  | Camofox `userId` Hermes uses when creating tabs. Setting this opts the session into "externally managed" mode.
L420: `browser.camofox.session_key`  | `CAMOFOX_SESSION_KEY`  | `sessionKey` (a.k.a. `listItemId`) sent on tab creation. Used to match an existing tab during adoption. Defaults to a per-task value if unset.
L421: `browser.camofox.adopt_existing_tab`  | `CAMOFOX_ADOPT_EXISTING_TAB`  | When true, Hermes calls `GET /tabs?userId=<user_id>` on first use and reuses an existing tab before creating a new one.
L422: Env vars take precedence over `config.yaml`. Either form works:
L423: 
L424:     `
L425: 
L426:     browser:
L427: 
L428:       camofox:
L429: 
L430:         user_id: shared-camofox
L431: 
L432:         session_key: visible-tab
L433: 
L434:         adopt_existing_tab: true
L435: 
L436:     `
L437: 
L438:     `
L439: 
L440:     REDACTED
L441: 
L442:     CAMOFOX_SESSION_KEY=visible-tab
L443: 
L444:     CAMOFOX_ADOPT_EXISTING_TAB=true
L445: 
L446:     `
L447: 
L448: What changes when `user_id` is set:
L449:   * Hermes skips destructive cleanup at task end (same as `managed_persistence: true`). The other app's tab/cookies/profile survive.
L450:   * Hermes does not call `DELETE /sessions/<user_id>` — that endpoint wipes all user data, so it would nuke the external app's session if it fired.
L451: 
L452: How tab adoption works (when `adopt_existing_tab: true`):
L453:   1. On the first browser tool call after a process start, Hermes issues `GET /tabs?userId=<user_id>` (5-second timeout).
L454:   2. If any tab in the response has `listItemId == session_key`, Hermes adopts the most recently created one in that group.
L455:   3. Otherwise, Hermes adopts the most recently created tab for the user (any `listItemId`).
L456:   4. If no tabs exist or the request fails, Hermes falls back to creating a new tab on the next operation.
L457: Adoption only fires until `tab_id` is populated for the session. If the external app closes the adopted tab mid-run, the next browser tool call will surface a Camofox error — Hermes does not re-poll for a fresh tab on every call.
L458: Picking `session_key`: if you want Hermes to reliably attach to a specific existing tab, set `session_key` to the `listItemId` the external app used when creating it. If you leave `session_key` unset and only set `user_id`, Hermes generates a per-task `session_key` (`task_<id>`) — Hermes will share cookies and the profile with the external app, but will open its own tab alongside instead of reusing one.
L459: Concurrency note: the external app and Hermes can drive the same Camofox `userId` simultaneously, but Camofox does not coordinate per-tab focus between clients. Coordinate ownership at the application layer (e.g. the external app pauses while Hermes runs).
L460: #### VNC live viewcite60†​ L461: 
L462: When Camofox runs in headed mode (with a visible browser window), it exposes a VNC port in its health check response. Hermes automatically discovers this and includes the VNC URL in navigation responses, so the agent can share a link for you to watch the browser live.
L463: ### Lightpanda local enginecite61†​ L464: 
L465: cite36†Lightpanda†lightpanda.io is an open-source headless browser written from scratch. It starts instantly, runs 9x faster and uses 16x less memory than Chrome, which matters for agents that live on small VMs for long stretches.

L467: 
L468:     `
L469: 
L470:     # Add to ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L471:
