citeturn1view0 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: find({"ref_id":"https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser/","pattern":"Browser Use mode"}); Total lines: 998
L18:       * cite10†Voice Mode L19:       * cite11†Wake Word L20:       * cite12†Web Search L21:       * cite13†X (Twitter) Search L22:       * cite14†Browser L41:   * cite29†Developer Guide L42: 
L43:   * cite30†Reference L44: 
L45: [Button: On this page]
L46: # Browser Automation
L47: 
L48: Hermes Agent includes a full browser automation toolset with multiple backend options:
L49:   * Browser Use cloud mode via cite31†Browser Use†browser-use.com for managed Chromium with stealth, residential proxies, CAPTCHA solving, and reusable browser profiles
L50:   * Browserbase cloud mode via cite32†Browserbase†browserbase.com as an alternative cloud browser provider with anti-bot tooling
L51:   * Browser Use mode via the cite33†Browser Use CLI 3.0†github.com , the default browser driver for local Chrome and Browser Use cloud browsers
L52:   * Firecrawl cloud mode via cite34†Firecrawl†firecrawl.dev for cloud browsers with built-in scraping
L53:   * Camofox local mode via cite35†Camofox†github.com for local anti-detection browsing (Firefox-based fingerprint spoofing)
L54:   * Lightpanda local engine via cite36†Lightpanda†lightpanda.io — a headless browser built from scratch in Zig for machines; instant start up, 16x lower memory and 9x faster than Chrome. Works in Browser Use mode (Hermes spawns it, no Chromium or Node needed) and with the built-in tools (automatic Chrome fallback for actions it doesn't support yet)
L55:   * Local Chromium-family CDP — connect browser tools to your own Chrome, Brave, Chromium, or Edge instance using `/browser connect`
L56:   * Local browser mode via the `agent-browser` CLI and a local Chromium installation
L57: In all modes, the agent can navigate websites, interact with page elements, fill forms, and extract information.
L58: ## Overviewcite37†​ L59: 
L60: Pages are represented as accessibility trees (text-based snapshots), making them ideal for LLM agents. Interactive elements get ref IDs (like `@e1`, `@e2`) that the agent uses for clicking and typing.
L61: 
L62: Key capabilities:
L63:   * Multi-provider cloud execution — Browser Use, Browserbase, or Firecrawl — no local browser needed
L64:   * Local Chromium-family integration — attach to your running Chrome, Brave, Chromium, or Edge browser via CDP for hands-on browsing
L65:   * Cloud anti-bot support — Browser Use Cloud includes stealth, residential proxies, and CAPTCHA solving
L66:   * Persistent cloud profiles — Browser Use Cloud can reuse cookies, localStorage, and saved passwords across sessions
L67:   * Session isolation — each task gets its own browser session
L68:   * Automatic cleanup — inactive sessions are closed after a timeout
L69:   * Vision analysis — screenshot + AI analysis for visual understanding
L70: ## Setupcite38†​ L71: 
L72: Nous Subscribers
L73: 
L74: If you have a paid cite39†Nous Portal†portal.nousresearch.com subscription, you can use browser automation through the cite7†Tool Gateway without any separate API keys. New installs can run `hermes setup --portal` to log in and turn on every gateway tool at once; existing installs can pick Nous Subscription as the browser provider via `hermes model` or `hermes tools`.
L75: ### Browser Use cloud modecite40†​ L76: 
L77: To use Browser Use as your cloud browser provider, add:
L78: 
L79:     `
L80: 
L81:     # Add to ~/.hermes/.env
L82: 
L83:     BROWSER_USE_API_KEY=***
L84: 
L85:     `
L86: 
L87: Get your API key at cite31†browser-use.com†browser-use.com .
L88: Browser Use Cloud runs managed Chromium with cite41†stealth†docs.browser-use.com and cite42†residential proxies†docs.browser-use.com enabled by default, includes CAPTCHA solving, and supports cite43†persistent profiles†docs.browser-use.com for cookies, localStorage, and saved passwords.
L89: ### Browserbase cloud modecite44†​ L90: 
L91: To use Browserbase-managed cloud browsers, add:
L92: 
L93:     `
L94: 
L95:     # Add to ~/.hermes/.env
L96: 
L97:     BROWSERBASE_API_KEY=***
L98: 
L99:     REDACTED
L100: 
L101:     `
L102: 
L103: Get your credentials at cite32†browserbase.com†browserbase.com .
L104: 
L105: Selecting the provider
L106: The `.env` keys above supply credentials only. The active cloud browser is chosen by the `browser.cloud_provider` selection written by `hermes tools` → Browser Automation (`browserbase`, `browser-use`, `camofox`, or `nous` for the Nous Subscription). Once a selection exists, adding or removing a key does not switch providers — and a selected provider with a missing key errors with guidance to run `hermes tools` instead of silently rerouting.
L107: Never-configured setups still autodetect from available credentials.
L108: ### Browser Use mode (default)cite45†​ L109: 
L110: Browser Use mode uses the cite33†Browser Use CLI 3.0†github.com instead of the built-in browser tools. The agent writes and executes Python in the browser to click, type, drag, scrape, and interact with webpages.
L111: This is the default browser mode: when `browser.backend` is unset, the agent gets the single `browser_exec` tool. Its engine is browser-harness (the Browser Use CLI is a thin wrapper around it), a regular Python dependency of Hermes, so every install ships it, including the Desktop app, with no separate download. If it is ever missing from Hermes's environment, Hermes falls back to the built-in browser tools and `hermes update` restores it.
L112: The mode is a driver that composes with your configured browser backend: it drives Hermes' own headless Chromium, a Nous-subscription cloud browser, Browserbase, Firecrawl, or Browser Use cloud browsers — whichever browser source is selected in `hermes tools` → Browser Automation. The one exception is Camofox, which has no CDP endpoint for the harness to attach to; Camofox setups automatically keep the built-in browser tools.
L113: Local browsing uses the packaged Chromium, not your own Chrome. With no cloud provider or `/browser connect` endpoint configured, Hermes launches the same Chromium that the built-in tools use (installed via `hermes tools` → Browser Automation, driven through agent-browser) and points the Browser Use CLI at it.
L114: Your installed Chrome is never touched, so there is no `chrome://inspect` remote-debugging toggle to enable and no "Allow remote debugging?" popup — and it works on headless hosts with no Chrome at all. The browser is shared with the built-in stack's lifecycle: it is closed after `browser.inactivity_timeout`, at exit, and by the orphan sweep. To drive a browser you're signed in to, use `/browser connect` or the cite46†real-profile toggle .
L115: Concurrent sessions: `browser_exec` accepts a `session=<name>` argument that isolates browser work per name on every backend. Each name gets its own harness daemon (its own IPC socket, log, and state) and its own browser (a separate packaged Chromium locally, a separate cloud browser on cloud backends) — so parallel subagents or simultaneous chats no longer clobber a single shared connection. Omitting `session` uses the shared default daemon, which is fine for one-at-a-time browsing.
L116: To opt out and force the built-in browser tools, use `/browser use off`, or:
L117: 
L118:     `
L119: 
L120:     # Add to ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L121: 
L122:     browser:
L123: 
L124:       backend: "off"
L125: 
L126:     `
L127: 
L128: (`backend: "browser-use"` remains valid to force the mode explicitly.)
L129: 
L130: Browser Use's own cloud browsers need `BROWSER_USE_API_KEY`; other browser sources use their existing credentials unchanged.
L131: 
L132: note
L133: Because Browser Use mode executes model-written Python on your machine, the `browser_exec` tool is only offered to sessions that also have terminal access. Platforms configured without the terminal toolset (e.g. a locked-down messaging surface) keep the default browser tools instead.
L134: ### Firecrawl cloud modecite47†​ L135: 
L136: To use Firecrawl as your cloud browser provider, add:
L137: 
L138:     `
L139: 
L140:     # Add to ~/.hermes/.env
L141: 
L142:     FIRECRAWL_API_KEY=fc-***
L143: 
L144:     `
L145: 
L146: Get your API key at cite34†firecrawl.dev†firecrawl.dev . Then select Firecrawl as your browser provider:
L147: 
L148:     `
L149: 
L150:     hermes setup tools
L151: 
L152:     # → Browser Automation → Firecrawl
L153: 
L154:     `
L155: Optional settings:
L156: 
L157:     `
L158: 
L159:     # Self-hosted Firecrawl instance (default: https://api.firecrawl.dev)
L160: 
L161:     FIRECRAWL_API_URL=http://localhost:3002
L162: 
L163:     # Session TTL in seconds (default: 300)
L164: 
L165:     FIRECRAWL_BROWSER_TTL=600
L166: 
L167:     `
L168: ### Hybrid routing: cloud for public URLs, local for LAN/localhostcite48†​ L169: 
L170: When a cloud provider is configured, Hermes auto-spawns a local Chromium sidecar for URLs that resolve to a private/loopback/LAN address (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `192.168.x.x`, `10.x.x.x`, `172.16-31.x.x`, `*.local`, `*.lan`, `*.internal`, IPv6 loopback `::1`, link-local `169.254.x.x`). Public URLs continue to use the cloud provider in the same conversation.
L171: This solves the common "I'm developing locally but using Browserbase" workflow — the agent can screenshot your dashboard at `http://localhost:3000` AND scrape `https://github.com` without you switching providers or disabling the SSRF guard. The cloud provider never sees the private URL.
L172: The feature is on by default. To disable it (all URLs go to the configured cloud provider, as before):
L173: 
L174:     `
L175: 
L176:     # ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L177: 
L178:     browser:
L179: 
L180:       cloud_provider: browserbase
L181: 
L182:       auto_local_for_private_urls: false
L183: 
L184:     `
L185: With auto-routing disabled, private URLs are rejected with `"Blocked: URL targets a private or internal address"` unless you also set `browser.allow_private_urls: true` (which lets the cloud provider attempt them — usually won't work since Browserbase etc. can't reach your LAN).
L186: Requirements: the local sidecar uses the same `agent-browser` CLI as pure local mode, so you need it installed (`hermes setup tools → Browser Automation` auto-installs it). Post-navigation redirects from a public URL onto a private address are still blocked (you can't use a redirect-to-internal trick to reach your LAN through the public path).
L218: A pin naming a profile directory that doesn't exist fails closed with a fixable message — it never silently falls back to the last-used profile.
L219: 
L220: When you turn the toggle back off, Hermes deletes the snapshot store (`~/.hermes/browser-profile/`) on the next browser use, so the copied credentials don't linger after you revoke consent.
L221: 
L222: A running browser can block the login/autofill databases
L231:   * Security framing: this is a consent-gated convenience, not an isolation boundary. A page the agent visits runs with your real logins, so only enable it when you want the agent acting as you. Off by default.
L232:   * Desktop: toggle it in Capabilities → Tools → Browser → Use My Real Browser Profile (the switch sits above the backend options), or in Settings → Config under the `browser` section.
L466: Lightpanda is a local engine (a browser source, like "Local Browser"), not a cloud provider. Install the binary and put it on your `PATH` (see the cite62†Lightpanda installation guide†lightpanda.io ), then pick Lightpanda in `hermes tools` → Browser Automation, or set:
L467: 
L468:     `
L469: 
L470:     # Add to ~/.hermes/config.yaml
L471: 
L472:     browser:
L473: 
L474:       cloud_provider: local
L475: 
L476:       engine: lightpanda
L477: 
L478:     `
L479: 
L480: Or via environment variable:
L481: 
L482:     `
L483: 
L484:     AGENT_BROWSER_ENGINE=lightpanda
L485: 
L486:     `
L487: The engine works with both browser drivers:
L488:   * Browser Use mode (the default). L191: * * *
L192: # Navigate the web like a human does.

L196: cite101†Explore more demos and prompts ↗†browser-use.com L197: > AI agents and crawlers: read cite102†browser-use.com/llms.txt†browser-use.com for the product map (open source, Browser Harness, Cloud browsers, Agents API, pricing) and cite103†docs.browser-use.com/llms.txt†docs.browser-use.com for the documentation index. Browser Use is the open-source browser agent (Python and TypeScript), a $0.02 per browser-hour cloud browser with stealth, CAPTCHA solving and residential proxies, and a hosted agent API.
L198: # Which Browser Use do I need?
L199: 
L200: cite104†Image: Three ways to use Browser Use: fully hosted cloud; your existing agent with Browser Use CLI; or the open source Browser Use agent, available as a Python library. The CLI and library each connect to a local or cloud browser. L201:   * cite105†Path 1: Fully Hosted Cloud : Scale up with a fully hosted agent and browser.
L202:   * cite106†Path 2: CLI : Automate your own browser tasks.
L203:   * cite107†Path 3: Python Library : Run the open source Browser Use agent locally from your own code.
L204: # Quickstart
L205: 
L206: ## Path 1: Fully Hosted Cloud
L207: 
L208: Scale browser automation with our hosted agent, stealth browsers, and infrastructure for profiles, recordings, and data policies.
L209: 
L210: cite108†Get started with the API ↗†docs.browser-use.com L211: 
L212: New Google, GitHub, or Microsoft signups get $15 cloud credit.
L213: ## Path 2: CLI
L214: 
L215: Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, or your favorite agent.
L216: 
L217:     `Install or upgrade browser-use to the latest stable version with uv using Python 3.12, run `browser-use skill install` to register the skill, and connect it to my browser. If setup or connection fails, follow https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.
L218:     `
L219: ## Path 3: Python Library
L220: 
L221: Run the Browser Use agent locally from Python, with your choice of model and a local or cloud browser:
L222: 
L223: 1. Install Browser Use (Python >= 3.11):
L224: 
L225: With cite109†uv†docs.astral.sh installed, run `uv init --python 3.12` first if you're starting a new project.
L226: 
L227:     uv add browser-use
L228: 
L229: 2. Add your cite110†OpenAI API key†platform.openai.com to `.env`:
L230: 
L231:     # .env
L232:     OPENAI_API_KEY=your-key
L233:     # BROWSER_USE_API_KEY=your-key  # Optional: BU2 model or cloud browser
L234: For either optional Browser Use service, get a cite111†Browser Use API key†cloud.browser-use.com .
L235: 3. Save this as `agent.py`:
L236: 
L237:     import asyncio
L238: 
L239:     from browser_use import Agent, Browser, ChatBrowserUse, ChatOpenAI
L240:     from dotenv import load_dotenv
L241: 
L242:     load_dotenv()
L243: 
L244:     async def main():
L245:         llm = ChatOpenAI(model='gpt-5.6-luna', reasoning_effort='xhigh')
L246:         # llm = ChatBrowserUse(model='bu-2-0')  # Use BU2 instead; requires BROWSER_USE_API_KEY
L247:         agent = Agent(
L248:             task="Find the number of stars of the browser-use repo",
L249:             llm=llm,
L250:             # browser=Browser(use_cloud=True),  # Use a cloud browser; requires BROWSER_USE_API_KEY
L251:         )
L252:         history = await agent.run()
L253:         print(history.final_result())
L254: 
L255:     if __name__ == "__main__":
L256:         asyncio.run(main())
L257: To use BU2, replace the `ChatOpenAI` line with the commented `ChatBrowserUse` line. The cloud-browser option works with either model.
L258: 
L259: 4. Run it:
L260: 
L261:     uv run agent.py
L262: 
L263: The agent opens a browser, looks up the repository, and prints its answer.
L264: 
L265: cite112†Python library docs ↗†docs.browser-use.com L266: # Anthropic SDK × Browser Use
L267: 
L268: Use Claude's browser toolset with Browser Use as the driver. Browser Use implements all 31 browser actions and can control a local browser, a Browser Use Cloud browser, or an existing remote browser over CDP. Bash is included in the Browser Use integration for processing data and writing files.
L269: Requires an Anthropic SDK version that includes `anthropic.tools.browser`. Bash requires a Linux or macOS host with `/bin/bash`; use WSL on Windows. The snippet below runs inside an async function; see the quickstart for a complete script.
L270: 
L271:     import os
L272: 
L273:     from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic
L274:     from browser_use.integrations.anthropic import Bash, BrowserUse
L275: 
L276:     task = 'Open example.com and report its page title.'
L277:     driver = BrowserUse()  # Or BrowserUse(use_cloud=True)
L278:     bash = Bash(output_dir='outputs')
L279: 
L280:     async with driver, AsyncAnthropic() as client:
L281:         runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner(
L282:             model=os.environ['ANTHROPIC_MODEL'],
L283:             max_tokens=32_768,
L284:             max_iterations=100,
L285:             tools=[driver, bash],
L286:             messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': task}],
L287:         )
L288:         result = await runner.until_done()
L289: cite113†Quickstart ↗ · cite114†Integration docs ↗†docs.browser-use.com L290: # Browser Use Benchmark v2
L291: 
L292: This cite115†very hard benchmark targets the hardest browser tasks. On easier tasks, even smaller models can achieve very high success rates. Results shown are from a 60-task subset of BU Bench V2.
L293: 
L294: ## Integrations, hosting, custom tools, MCP, and more on our cite116†Docs ↗†docs.browser-use.com L295: # FAQ
L296: 
L297: Should I use the fully hosted cloud, CLI, or Python library?
L298: 
L299:   * cite105†Fully Hosted Cloud : Send tasks through the API and let Browser Use run the agent, browser, and infrastructure.
L300:   * cite106†CLI : Give an existing agent (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, OpenClaw, Pi, Cursor, etc.) browser access. You can use it interactively or in scripts.
L301:   * cite107†Python Library : Run the open source agent in your own application, with custom tools, structured output, and your choice of model.
L302: The CLI and Python library can each connect to a local or cloud browser. A cloud browser hosts the browser; the fully hosted API runs the agent as well.
L303: 
"}

The existing host installation occupies approximately 0.20 GiB for the Python environment, 0.32 GiB for source excluding `.git`, and 0.03 GiB for the lab home, measured from allocated file blocks; shared/hard-linked blocks may be counted more than once. These numbers do not measure the additional Linux VM, Linux dependencies, container images or browser. Size those artifacts and allow build/extraction headroom before setting a replacement free-space target; do not substitute another unmeasured hard minimum. verification/RUNTIME_SETUP.md:38:On 2026-10-04, a new allocated-block measurement found 0.202 GiB for the Python environment, 0.324 GiB for upstream source excluding `.git`, and 0.042 GiB for the lab home (about 0.57 GiB combined). This excludes installed Chrome, Git history and shared caches, and may double-count hard links. Free disk was 4.19 GiB at that instant and varies with other activity. The official pinned amd64 image has about 0.90 GiB of compressed layers according to registry metadata; expanded layers and VM overhead remain unmeasured. See [the image lock](../deployment/cloudflare/runtime/README.md). The native browser resource probe reuses installed Chrome and does not create a Linux VM or download model weights.
verification/RUNTIME_SETUP.md:76:This prepares a Linux VM/container runtime boundary. Distinct Hermes `HERMES_HOME` directories alone remain configuration separation. The eventual two-owner test must place the complete runtime, browser/MCP processes, credentials, workspace, memory, sessions, and artifacts inside separate owner containers and prove cross-owner access is denied.
